news.title: AOC’s Low Favorability Complicates Democrats’ Push for Change: Poll
news.text: A new national poll reveals that while a majority of Democrats are eager for sweeping changes within their party, high-profile progressive leader Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez faces low favorability ratings that could complicate her emergence as a unifying national figure. The CNN/SSRS survey, which was conducted between July 23-27, found that a majority of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents favor significant changes to the party's leadership and strategic direction. At the same time, the poll registered a 26 percent national favorability rating for Ocasio-Cortez, one of the party’s most prominent progressive voices. Her unfavorable rating was at 36 percent. Among adults ages 18 to 34—a demographic frequently viewed as a core source of support for the New York Democrat—her favorability stood at 28 percent. The congresswoman's favorability went up to 30 percent among those aged 35 to 49. The poll surveyed 1,225 respondents, with the margin of error being +/-3.2 at the 95 percent confidence level. The findings underscore a complex strategic dilemma for Democrats as they grapple with their future. While rank-and-file voters express widespread dissatisfaction with current leadership, the data indicates that high visibility has not yet translated into broad national appeal for one of the party's most prominent alternatives. Ocasio-Cortez has repeatedly stated she is not running for president in 2028, though she remains a leading voice in the party's progressive wing and a prolific national fundraiser. Newsweek has reached out to Ocasio-Cortez's office and the Democratic National Committee for comment via email and contact form respectively. A Divided Electorate and the Search for Direction According to the survey, roughly one-third of Democrats identify as democratic socialists, underscoring the enduring influence of progressive ideology within the coalition. Concurrently, a broad majority favors replacing existing leadership and overhauling the party's approach. However, Ocasio-Cortez's public standing remains polarized. Despite her large social media following and her significant fundraising ability, her 26 percent favorability rating trails the typical marks of nationally prominent politicians with presidential-level name recognition, who historically register positive ratings in the 40 to 50 percent range depending on the political environment. What Have Potential Democratic Frontrunners for 2028 Said The 2028 Democratic presidential race is still in its early stages, with no major candidates having formally announced campaigns, but several figures have already emerged as potential contenders. Vice President Kamala Harris, who has traveled to states like Michigan and South Carolina in recent months, suggested she could run again without making a formal announcement. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked whether she planned to run for president in 2028 during the National Action Network’s annual convention. Harris noted she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office. I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires,” she said. California Governor Gavin Newsom discussed the possibility of running in a June 2025 interview with The Wall Street Journal. “I'm not thinking about running, but it's a path that I could see unfold,” he said. Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to President Barack Obama, earlier this year. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff has said he is not planning to run, telling CNN, “I am not running for president in 2028, I have no interest in running for president in 2028.” He said he is “laser-focused” on winning reelection in Georgia this year in a race the Cook Political Report forecasts as "Lean Democratic." What Happens Next With the next presidential election a couple of years away, party strategists note that Democrats face a dual imperative: satisfying a restless base demanding structural reform while identifying standard-bearers capable of building consensus across a diverse electoral coalition. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: A new poll found Ocasio-Cortez's low favorability rating may complicate her emergence as a unifying figure within the party.
news.author: Hannah Parry

news.title: Iran suspected in cyberattack on US water systems across at least seven states
news.text: A cyberattack has affected water systems in at least seven U.S. states, and the full scope of the damage may be larger, The New York Times reported. Minnesota was the first state to disclose incidents involving its water infrastructure, followed by Michigan. No formal federal announcement has identified the attacker, but Iran has emerged as the leading suspect in the preliminary investigation. The FBI and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday that water systems in at least seven states had reported incidents to federal authorities. Officials said there was no indication that drinking-water supplies had been contaminated or disrupted. Utilities across the country were nevertheless preparing for possible failures in the computer systems used to monitor water quality and chemical levels. American officials described the scale of the attack as unprecedented. Iran, however, has previously been linked to attempts to compromise water infrastructure abroad. In 2020, ynet reported that Iran had carried out a cyberattack against Israeli water facilities. A Western intelligence official later told the Financial Times that the operation was intended to increase chlorine levels in water supplied to Israeli homes. Four Israeli officials and one Western official said at the time that the attackers had penetrated software controlling Israeli water pumps after routing their activity through American and European servers to conceal the code’s origin. According to the Western official, the attack could have caused the pumps to shut down once abnormal chemical readings were detected. That could have left thousands of Israelis without running water during a heat wave. U.S. authorities have not concluded that the latest attack was directed by Iran. Officials emphasized that the investigation remains in its early stages and that cyber investigations can take months before firm conclusions are reached. The New York Times reported that Iran has intensified cyber activity against American targets since the war involving Israel and the United States began. Iranian hackers have also previously attempted to target similar water facilities in the U.S. The newspaper said the incidents did not appear to be financially motivated, reducing the likelihood that ordinary cybercriminals were responsible. President Donald Trump played down the reports Friday and questioned whether Iran had carried out the attack. “I think Minnesota is behind it,” Trump said. “I don’t believe there was an Iranian cyberattack.” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, who served as Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris’ running mate in the most recent election, rejected Trump’s remarks. “This is what modern warfare looks like,” Walz said. After Trump spoke, federal officials said privately that Iran remained the main suspect, though they stressed that investigators had not yet obtained conclusive evidence. Nate George, mayor of Braham, a small city north of Minneapolis reportedly targeted in the operation, told The New York Times that local and federal authorities had little doubt about who was responsible. “We are getting bits and pieces of information from the state of Minnesota and the FBI,” he said. George, a Republican running for Minnesota state auditor, said authorities were “pretty confident” that Iranian actors were behind the attack but were reluctant to say so publicly. Federal officials declined to identify all the affected states. Michigan, however, confirmed that several communities had reported incidents resembling those described by federal agencies. “We have received a small number of reports from communities in Michigan indicating activity consistent with what federal agencies have described,” state spokesperson Dale George said. He added that all affected systems continued to operate safely and that there were “no known impacts posing a public-health concern.” Alex Orleans, a former U.S. government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, said Tehran has carried out a wide range of operations against American, Israeli and other Middle Eastern targets since the war began. The intrusion into American water systems appeared to mark a major escalation, he said. “What is unprecedented here is that we are seeing direct, tangible effects on control systems inside critical U.S. infrastructure,” Orleans told The New York Times. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Friday that hackers had targeted “water facilities of all sizes.” It advised operators to disconnect potentially vulnerable controllers from the internet. The attack had resulted in boil-water notices and the continued manual operation of some systems, the agency said. Former intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts said the hackers most likely exploited available vulnerabilities rather than selecting particular cities for strategic reasons. The reports come amid growing tensions in the Middle East and speculation that military operations against Iran could soon resume. CBS reported Saturday that an Israeli official said Israel was unaware of any decision to fully renew the military campaign and had not been asked to participate in military action against Iran. Israel has maintained public silence while waiting for a decision from the White House and seeking to avoid being portrayed as pressing for a wider war. American embassies across the region, including in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Israel, have issued security warnings urging U.S. citizens to leave or prepare for immediate departure in the event of further escalation.
news.summary: The FBI and environmental regulators are investigating incidents affecting facilities of different sizes, while officials say water supplies remain safe and caution that no definitive attribution has been made

When I think about what he did in terms of investing in the people during dire times and talking about the role and responsibility of government, that it should not just be about the benevolence of community organizations or just interpersonal relationships. The government has a role. I think he was a very important president."

Harris then praised John F. Kennedy and Lyndon B. Johnson.

"I credit Kennedy, of course, in terms of what he laid the groundwork for," she said. "And then Johnson followed up on [it]."Barack Obama Earns High PraiseHarris also singled out former President Barack Obama, calling him "one of the greatest presidents" for his work on healthcare reform.

"And then of course, Barack Obama and what he did with the Affordable Care Act, among many things," she said. "But in particular, if we had one issue that's been ailing America for generations, which is a healthcare system that has failed anyone other than the rich, and addressing the way that he did and took a lot of heat for it, I think he's one of the greatest presidents."Joe Biden Left Off the ListWhile Harris praised Roosevelt, Kennedy, Johnson and Obama, she never mentioned Biden — the president she served under from 2021 to 2025.

The omission was particularly notable given Biden selected Harris as his running mate in 2020 and later endorsed her to replace him atop the Democratic ticket after ending his own reelection campaign.The 2024 Campaign ShakeupBiden withdrew from the 2024 race three weeks after a widely criticized debate performance against Donald Trump, during which he delivered a rambling response about the national debt.

After stepping aside, Biden threw his support behind Harris, who inherited much of his campaign infrastructure and mounted an abbreviated campaign against Trump. 

She ultimately lost both the Electoral College and the popular vote, though speculation continues that she could mount another White House bid in 2028.

news.title: AOC’s Chances of Beating Newsom and Harris in New 2028 Michigan Poll
news.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been increasingly mentioned as a prominent potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, but a newly released poll indicates she would encounter a competitive primary field. A hypothetical Democratic primary survey conducted by The Public Sentiment Institute (TPSI), between July 25-29 among 762 likely voters in Michigan, reveals former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg leading potential candidates with 24.2 percent support. Meanwhile, 21.7 percent of respondents remain undecided, underscoring the volatility characteristic of the race's early stages. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff secured second place among named candidates with 13.9 percent, closely followed by New York's Ocasio-Cortez at 10.7 percent. California Governor Gavin Newsom registered 10.0 percent, and former Vice President Kamala Harris captured 5.1 percent support. Additional contenders included Illinois Governor JB Pritzker at 3.8 percent and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro at 3.6 percent. The poll's margin of error was plus or minus 4 points at 95 percent confidence. While these figures position Ocasio-Cortez as a notable presence within the party, they show her trailing several high-profile rivals in a crowded landscape. Newsweek reached out to Ocasio-Cortez’s office via email on Saturday for comment. Prediction Markets Show a Competitive Democratic Contest Early prediction markets also suggest there is no clear frontrunner for the 2028 Democratic nomination. Markets tracking the race on platforms including Polymarket and Kalshi have shown fluctuating odds among a number of possible candidates, reflecting uncertainty over who will ultimately enter the contest and how the Democratic electorate’s priorities may shift over the next two years. While prediction markets can provide insight into public sentiment and trader expectations, they are not polls and do not represent a direct measure of voter support. On Polymarket, it shows as of Saturday morning, that Newsom has a 19 percent chance, Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff at 14 percent, Harris with 9 percent, Buttigieg and Shapiro with 5 percent, and Pritzker with a 1 percent chance. As of Saturday morning, on Kalshi, it shows Newsom at 18 percent, Ossoff at 15 percent, Ocasio-Cortez at 13 percent, Harris at 9.3 percent, Buttigieg at 5.5 percent, Shapiro at 4.5 percent, and Pritzker at 2.7 percent. What 2028 Democratic Contenders Have Said About Their Plans Harris, who has traveled to states like Michigan and South Carolina in recent months, suggested she could run again without making a formal announcement. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked whether she planned to run for president in 2028 during the National Action Network’s annual convention. Harris noted she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office. I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires,” she said. Newsom discussed the possibility of running in a June 2025 interview with The Wall Street Journal. “I'm not thinking about running, but it's a path that I could see unfold,” he said. Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to President Barack Obama, earlier this year. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." Ossoff has said he is not planning to run, telling CNN, “I am not running for president in 2028, I have no interest in running for president in 2028.” He said he is “laser-focused” on winning reelection in Georgia this year in a race the Cook Political Report forecasts as "Lean Democratic." Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Matthew Robinson and Anthony Murray.

news.title: Trump’s legal crusade against news media falters
news.text: NEW YORK — Donald Trump’s early legal wins against broadcasters ABC and CBS have given way to defeats and retreats as courts and newsrooms act to protect press freedom.“News organizations recognize that the only positive outcome to this is prevailing against the president and standing up for the reporters and their newsrooms,” said Ken Paulson, director of the Free Speech Center at Middle Tennessee State University.At the end of July, the Justice Department withdrew subpoenas issued to New York Times journalists who had written articles about the security of Trump’s presidential aircraft.It was forced to act after a federal judge slammed the administration’s sloppy legal work and found it violated protections granted to journalists and their sources.The president has also filed defamation suits targeting The New York Times over articles and a book about the origins of his fortune, and the Wall Street Journal over an article about a salacious letter he sent to Jeffrey Epstein. Both are floundering.“If you’re willing to stand up to Trump, you’re going to do fairly well in court, given the lack of merit behind the cases that he has filed,” observes Dan Kennedy, a journalism professor at Northeastern University in Massachusetts.The cases involving ABC and CBS ended in December 2024 and July 2025, with the broadcasters promising to pay $15 million and $16 million, respectively.Trump sued ABC for defamation over statements about a civil judgment against Trump in a sexual assault case. He took CBS to court for allegedly misleading viewers by airing different clips of the same answer from an interview with 2024 Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.But most legal experts agree that the courts could have thrown out Trump’s claims.Both reached the settlements “for business reasons,” said Kennedy.CBS’s parent company Paramount Global, for instance, was seeking regulatory approval for its merger with Skydance.Media strategyAfter ABC kept talk-show host Jimmy Kimmel, a nightly critic of Trump, on the air, and elected not to air a live Trump speech about supposed electoral fraud, the network now faces threats to some of its local station licenses from federal authorities.In another case, the BBC, which the US president is suing for $10 billion over an allegedly misleading edit of one of his speeches, has adopted a strategy that experts expect to become more widespread.The British broadcaster is demanding that Trump’s legal team produce financial documents in order to quantify the damages suffered.“That is the biggest deterrent of all for a man who has constantly resisted efforts to look inside his empire and financial circumstances,” said Paulson.Trump’s real objective, however, is not to win the lawsuits, experts say.“You go right back to the beginning of his political career, 11-12 years ago, and it’s been a central part of his strategy to discredit the news media,” said Kennedy.“He does that by insulting them, calling them fake news, calling them enemies of the people, and he does it by filing lawsuits.”Paulson said that “Trump and his lawyers have no realistic expectation that they will prevail in a court of law somewhere down the road.”“But that can take years and millions of dollars, and Trump knows from his business experience that if he can apply enough pressure, someone will cough up a check.”

news.title: Kamala Harris Asked Who ‘Most Effective’ Presidents Were. Doesn’t Mention Former Boss
news.text:

news.title: Roadblock to White House: AOC’s favorables dive even as New Hampshire tempts her
news.text:
AOC’s appeal among young voters around the country is losing some of its shine – even as socialists score wins across the country and she climbs in a crucial presidential battleground.

A CNN/SSRS poll released Thursday revealed Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), 36, one of the original “Squad” members, is having trouble keeping her appeal among the young.

Only 28% of voters in the 18-34 bracket give her a favorable rating. Her numbers are worse among politically vital independents, where she scores just 22%, according to data reported by Puck News.

Her overall approval rating is 26%, compared to 36% who have an unfavorable view of her – leaving her 10 points underwater. Back in January, her favorable rating was slightly higher at 27%, while her unfavorable rating was at 32%.

By comparison, her New York comrade Mayor Mamdani enjoys a slightly better 30% favorable opinion, compared to 35% who have an unfavorable opinion of him.

The national reality check comes days after a new University of New Hampshire poll had her leading the Democratic field in the early primary state – with 22% support. She was followed by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (21%) and Sen. Mark Kelly (9%).

Buttigieg came in second to AOC’s democratic socialist mentor, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), in 2020. Sanders defeated Sen. Hillary Clinton there four years earlier, while ultimately losing the nomination both times.

“She’s a brand. She’s far more than a House member,” said Dante Scala, a professor of political science at UNH. “Who knows what her plans are, but right now she’s set up to be the successor to Bernie Sanders.”

Nationally, according to the CNN poll, AOC’s favorable rating trails the Republican Party (31%) and the Democratic Party (30%), although she is more popular than the Democratic Socialists of America, which gets just 18% favorability despite scoring key election wins in New York, Colorado, and other states.

Just 25% of men have a favorable view of her, compared to 27% of women, 25% of whites.

She gets 36% favorable support from white college grads, and 63% of liberals, but only 22% of independents have a favorable view of her, compared to 56% of Democrats.

The DSA’s new platform, which calls for abolishing the Senate and defunding the Pentagon, has drawn pushback from other Democrats in New York and elsewhere.

The same poll showed about a third of Democrats and Democrat-leaners now identify as democratic socialists.

New Hampshire for decades has had an outsized role in the nominating process, although a Democratic National Committee panel voted late last month to have South Carolina, which has a more racially diverse electorate, go first.

AOC’s 22% support in that poll climbed from 15% in Februrary and 14% in October 2025.

But her road to the White House is far from set, as she ponders whether to challenge Sen. Charles Schumer, 75, in 2028. She trailed former VP Kamala Harris (26%), California Gov. Gavin Newsom (20%), and Buttigieg (10%) in a national Morning Consult poll released last week.
news.summary: AOC's appeal among young voters is losing some of its shine – even as socialists score wins across the country and she rises among primary voters in a crucial presidential battleground.

news.title: The surreal plot behind Trump’s new Smithsonian labels
news.text:
“Who controls the past controls the future. Who controls the present controls the past.” — George Orwell, 1984

It seemed so trivial. Trump ordered the Interior Department to post signs along the walkways leading up to several of the museums that make up the Smithsonian system in Washington, DC warning people that they’d find “inaccurate information” therein. It was based on a bizarre “report” written by the White House’s Domestic Policy Council and released without fanfare on the 4th of July.

The Council itself was packed with Trump with leftovers from rightwing think tanks and activist groups like American Compass, Heritage, the Manhattan Institute, and Stephen Miller’s America First Policy Institute. 

It claims that the American Museum of American History has displays that cover the fights for women’s and civil rights and to end slavery along with the positive role immigrants, women, and queer people have played in our country, which it finds deplorable and un-American. It wrote that Smithsonian leadership and museum curators:

“…have directed the museum’s mission away from historical education and scholarship of a shared national inheritance to be celebrated, and toward extreme political activism, rooted in Marxism, to divide, dispirit and discourage Americans. … [And have] denigrated and displaced whites, males, Christians and Americans” while focusing on “race in areas where it has little to no historical relevance.”

Wild, over-the-top complaints that our museums are accurately portraying American history notwithstanding, this is far more sinister and dire than it seems.

Pretty much every dictator in history, both ancient and modern, has rewritten his nation’s history because, as Orwell noted, those who control the past can use it to reprogram the future.

Dictators and wannabe dictators rewrite the past to legitimize their rule, typically portraying themselves as representing the inevitable culmination of history, as the nation’s savior (“I, alone, can fix it!”), and as the rightful heir to a mythical glorious tradition like Trump is doing by trying to reinvent America as an exclusively white Christian nation.

In the process, they typically erase their rivals (Trump has replaced Biden’s picture in the White House with a photo of an autopen), reframe negatively their political opponents (ditto), and use the threat of erasure from history as a weapon against their own allies to keep them bowing and scraping (ditto).

Dictatorial regimes frequently use rewritten history to justify wars of aggression, suppress minorities, and gut civil liberties. Modern American examples include how Sam Alito cited a 17th century witch-hanging British judge to justify ripping the right to abortion away from women, or how Trump has reinvented (with extensive lies) Obama’s peace deal with Iran to justify his and Netanyahu’s illegal war.

They rewrite history to bind themselves to the country’s majority group with simplified stories of the nation’s “glorious” past, claiming members of that group must rally around them to maintain national unity, strength, and a shared destiny. Diversity, in this context, is seen as a weakness as it doesn’t support this kind of dictatorial framing, which is why Trump called Kamala Harris “a DEI hire” on the campaign trail and has essentially criminalized the phrase.

Rewriting history is also a powerful way to shift the Overton Window to the right, causing the previously unthinkable to become “common sense.” When the history of protest, democratic movements, and civil rights efforts are reframed as chaos or crises in the nation’s history, young people are less likely to engage in them. When citizens fail to learn about successful alternatives to authoritarian rule, it can make democracy or pluralism seem unnatural or even impossible, particularly to young people.

— When Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BCE, he rewrote Egyptian history to make himself the son of the god Amun, the seniormost of the gods and arguably the one we acknowledge to this day when we end a prayer by invoking his name. — Joseph Stalin removed purged officials from photographs, rewrote textbooks, and reshaped official government accounts of the Russian Revolution and WWI to magnify his own role. — Adolf Hitler and his Nazi regime taught a racialized version of German history that portrayed Jews, Slavs, Gypsies, and other racial and political minority groups as enemies and Germany as the victim of a “stabbed in the back” betrayal after World War I. — Mao Zedong oversaw repeated revisions of Chinese history, especially after the Cultural Revolution, with history textbooks and official records regularly being edited or radically changed to meet his political needs. To this day, for example, they’ve elided the Tiananmen Square Massacre.— Even small-timers like Saddam Hussein do this; he linked himself to ancient Mesopotamian rulers and promoted a personality cult through museums, monuments, giant banners with his face on them hanging from federal buildings, and school curricula.

The simple reality is that in democracies it’s historians, journalists, courts, archives, universities, and scholars who write history and can challenge official narratives. Debate is expected, and interpretations can change as new evidence comes to light, like we saw here recently with the 1619 Project.

In dictatorships, on the other hand, the state typically monopolizes education, media, and archives, suppresses competing interpretations of history, and punishes those who publicly contradict the official version.

All of which is why it’s so important that we don’t treat the efforts by Trump and his neofascist lickspittles to rewrite America’s history into a sanitized white male supremacist mold as if it’s just some sort of aberration or sick joke. 

This is serious stuff, and serious people within this administration are dedicated to destroying our and — particularly — our children’s understanding of the truly revolutionary and progressive history of this nation. 

They’re trying to induce a national amnesia, stretching back through the history of the Klan, the Civil War, and even the American Revolution.

We must push back against them boldly and loudly, and when they’re gone we’re going to have a huge job cleaning up the fascist mess they’re making.

I don't know if they're going to do something to me or my family or my community. There's a real fear that we're living with." "What I'm most afraid of is the fact that so many of the people in my community, so many people in the district, voted for her," he added. Many residents are still reeling from the deadly antisemitic attack in Boulder last year. In June 2025, an 82-year-old woman, Karen Diamond, was killed and a dozen others were injured when a man threw Molotov cocktails into a peaceful pro-Israel gathering on Boulder’s Pearl Street Mall. Prosecutors charged 45-year-old illegal immigrant Mohamed Sabry Soliman with murder and hate crimes, noting he yelled "Free Palestine" and spent a year planning the attack to "kill all Zionist people." When asked about the attack during a 9News interview, Kiros condemned the violence but refused to call it antisemitic, saying she didn’t "know what was in the heart of the perpetrator." A few weeks after the 9News interview, Kiros clarified that the attack in Boulder was indeed "a horrific attack on a group of Jewish people that were peacefully protesting," but she blamed Israel for rising antisemitism in the U.S. THE GREAT BETRAYAL: HOW RADICAL PROGRESSIVES ARE DYNAMITING THE BLACK-JEWISH ALLIANCE "We are seeing that the actions of Israel are putting Jewish people in great danger," she continued, while vowing to prioritize combating "hate and antisemitism" if elected. For some advocates in Denver’s Jewish community, her refusal to label the attack as antisemitic was seen as a slap in the face. "Kiros's inability to call the Boulder firebombing an antisemitic attack was extremely frustrating and difficult for our community to hear," Brandon Rattiner, senior director of the Jewish Community Relations Council (JCRC), told Fox News Digital. "First and foremost, she's a lawyer, and the judge said it was an antisemitic attack, so this is not something that’s really still being debated." "The impact here was pretty clear: A Jewish person was killed, over a dozen were hurt, and it was one of the biggest and most prominent antisemitic attacks on Jews throughout the world," he continued. "So the inability to see and to hear our community when we are asking for level of care and empathy was incredibly hurtful to hear." Rattiner met with Kiros ahead of the primary to share his community’s concerns. While he thought they had a good conversation, Rattiner said he felt betrayed when Kiros appeared on anti-Israel podcaster Hasan Piker’s livestream two weeks later and "did the opposite of everything that we had discussed." "I had asked for nuance and she spoke in absolutist positions," Rattiner said. "I had asked for empathy and compassion, and she seemed to only allow that for one side of the conflict." Kiros, a former attorney turned doctoral student and barista, launched her campaign on progressive promises like universal healthcare, housing reform, and universal child and elder care. But her positions on Israel became a polarizing flashpoint. While national progressives view her win as proof that voters want bolder policies, local Jewish leaders say that normalizing extreme language makes everyday life less safe for their community. Susan Rona, regional director for the Anti-Defamation League (ADL), told Fox News Digital that this rhetoric fuels violence against Jewish people. "When political leaders refuse to name something as a targeted antisemitic attack, it creates some distrust of leadership and causes additional fear because it minimizes and causes dehumanization of Jews, which leads to violence," Rona said. "We’re seeing that pretty clearly in Colorado," she continued. "There’s a direct line to all this antisemitic rhetoric we’re hearing and violence happening toward the Jewish community." Antisemitic incidents are skyrocketing in Colorado, according to the advocacy group, having reached the third-highest on record since ADL began tracking them in 1979. ADL’s most recent report tallied 167 incidents in 2025 — a massive jump from ten years ago when the region saw fewer than 12 cases in a year. What makes 2026 particularly alarming, Rona said, is the rise in the violent nature of these attacks. She cited the Boulder firebombing, a child being physically assaulted with a makeshift lasso and subject to antisemitic slurs, and a visibly Jewish woman being assaulted in a laundromat. The ADL says that criticism of Zionism and the state of Israel is central to the Democratic Socialists of America’s platform. The ADL released an update to its report on the DSA political movement after its wave of primary wins this year, highlighting the DSA’s "explicitly anti-Israel platform." The report noted the DSA’s formal endorsement of Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) against Israel, and declaration that Zionism is equivalent to racism. According to ADL, at its national convention, the DSA also passed a resolution mandating that its candidates refuse any affiliation with "Zionist lobby groups" or the Israeli government. "I'm concerned that antisemitism is becoming mainstreamed in politics. It's becoming institutionalized [and] normalized," Rona said. Community leaders stressed that their issue isn't simply disagreeing with someone over their criticism of Israel or its leadership. "It is always OK to criticize Israel the same way it's OK to criticize any country; that is part of the democratic process," Rabbi Lehrfield said. "There's nobody more critical of Israel than Israelis… But there's a big distinction between criticizing Israel and demonizing it and saying it doesn't have a right to exist." "When it turns into hate speech and starts this normalization of targeting and dehumanizing Jews, it's where we really [cross] a line, and we have to call it out for what it is," Rona agreed. Not everyone agrees that Kiros’ rhetoric is anti-Jewish. Ian Zuckerman, an associate professor of history at Regis University who says he’s a "proudly Jewish Coloradan," published an op-ed in Colorado Newsline saying he was "thrilled" by Kiros’ primary win. He adamantly disagreed with those who called her rhetoric antisemitic, using examples from history to say that a rejection of political Zionism is not equivalent to antisemitism. He accused the candidate's critics of "splitting hairs," arguing Kiros did ultimately condemn the violent attack against individuals over their beliefs. "Kiros got it right: Respect for basic human dignity means that no one should be subjected to violence because of their beliefs or their ascriptive identity," he wrote. "Though the scale is incomparable, our condemnation of the attacks in Boulder and our horror at the genocide in Gaza stem from the same moral principle." In response to Kiros’ victory, a Jewish independent candidate, Dr. Shimon Blau, quickly gathered signatures to get on the ballot for the general election. While winning a third-party campaign in Denver is an uphill battle, Rattiner said his candidacy speaks volumes about the mood of the electorate. "The best way to understand his candidacy is this is a community that is feeling isolated, vilified, and in pain," Rattiner said. Blau called Kiros’ campaign a danger to the Jewish community. He also suggested he was entering the race to stand up against socialist policies. "I believe in human rights for everyone," Blau told the Denverite. "I believe in healthcare reform, in fiscal responsibility. I believe in a certain level of personal responsibility, and I'm a little bit wary of government overreach if it's a little bit too far. I am absolutely not a socialist." Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77 percent of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado. Despite the tension, some community leaders like Rattiner say they aren't giving up on dialogue if Kiros is elected in November. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The Jewish community doesn't want to be in a state of permanent warfare with any representative," Rattiner said. "I sincerely hope that Melat Kiros will listen to our community and educate herself about the policies and positions that she has and the implications in the Jewish community. But I think what she may have even more of an opportunity to do is use her credibility on the left to help elevate concerns of the Jewish people so that when the Jewish people do call out in pain, when they express their fear and concern, it's not written off." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats, and the Working Families Party. She became the 28th candidate endorsed by a far-left group to win a Democratic primary election this cycle as the socialist movement continues to increase its influence across the nation. Kiros' campaign, Shimon Blau, and the DSA did not return Fox News Digital’s requests for comment.
news.summary: Denver's Jewish leaders say Melat Kiros's primary upset and sharp anti-Israel rhetoric are fueling antisemitic incidents and real fear in their community.

news.title: Ramaswamy outlines key contrasts with Dem opponent less than 100 days out from key gubernatorial election
news.text: HAMILTON, OHIO - Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy gave Fox News Digital an update on his campaign roughly 100 days from the midterms and said the contrast between him and his opponent was on display at Dr. Anthony Fauci’s controversial Senate hearing this week. "I think if every person in Ohio votes for the candidate who's going to bring high-paying jobs most quickly to our state, we're going to win in a decisive victory," Ramaswamy said at the Butler County Fair on Wednesday after speaking to an enthusiastic crowd of roughly 100 people. "And my pledge is really simple, lower costs, that's lower electric bills, lower property taxes and lower healthcare expenses, bigger paychecks, more high paying jobs in the state and better schools by bringing standards back to public education. And one of the things I've seen is that that's a message that isn't just limited to Republicans, it's resonating with voters across the state." One of the most talked about issues at the fair, including two attendees who spoke to Fox News Digital, was property taxes and which candidate would best address that growing and often disruptive expense. MORENO UNLOADS ON FAUCI AFTER SENATE HEARING, CALLS HIM DEMOCRATS' 'HERO' OVER PANDEMIC POLICIES "The top issues that people are struggling with is number one, the property tax burden, it's gotten way too high," Ramaswamy said when asked what he’s hearing most from voters in terms of what they are most concerned about. "We've laid out a practical plan to give the biggest property tax relief package Ohio's ever seen. Number two is the electric bills, which have gone up way too quickly. It more than doubled in many parts of the state. Producing more energy and ending load forecasting inflation, those are things that a governor actually can do. And that's something that I'm gonna lead with." Ramaswamy added that the third issue he hears most from voters is healthcare costs and the overall cost of living. "The number one way I'm going to be able to address that is by raising take-home pay, both by bringing more high-paying jobs to the state, but also by allowing Ohioans to keep more of what they earn by becoming a zero-income tax state, just like Texas and Florida and Tennessee, Ohio can be that state and I'm confident I'll be able to put the state on a path to get there starting next year." RAMASWAMY: MEDICAID FRAUD RAISES HEALTHCARE COSTS FOR HARDWORKING OHIOANS Fauci made headlines this week after invoking the Fifth Amendment over 100 times during a Senate hearing on his handling of the coronavirus, a moment Ramaswamy told the crowd as well as Fox News Digital relates to his opponent Dr. Amy Acton’s time as director of the Ohio Department of Health from 2019 to 2020. Ramaswamy pointed to a comment from Acton, which Fox News Digital reported on earlier this month, claiming the COVID mortality rate was at 50% when in reality it was significantly lower. Acton’s campaign responded saying she had been referring to death rates in hospitals and that she "worked to keep Ohioans safe." "I think people look at that and say, is that somebody who has the kind of character that has the capacity to deal with data and make objective decisions and lead?" Ramaswamy explained. "And while those questions are playing out for Anthony Fauci at the national level, I think they're really resonating right here in Ohio. You could walk around and you could even see some of the signs at this fair that are protesting the decisions she made because she actually wanted Ohio to shut down county fairs while still allowing BLM protests to rage wild on the streets at the same time in the name of science. That's not objective decision-making." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ramaswamy is making the case that Ohioans are "rejecting that mentality" in favor of "common sense." Polling suggests that the race between Ramaswamy and Acton will be a tight race with the Real Clear Politics average of polling showing a dead heat despite President Trump winning Ohio by commanding margins in the past three presidential election cycles, including by 12 points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

news.title: “If I Prove That You Can Win Statewide Taking on AIPAC, That is Catastrophic”
news.text:
On July 8, Abdul El-Sayed had just wrapped up a campaign stop inside a sweltering church auditorium in Ferndale, Michigan. The room was packed with supporters fanning themselves with campaign signs, many braving the summer heat to hear the progressive Senate candidate make his case against his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens.

Then came the applause.

It wasn’t for Medicare for All or his warnings about the rise of data centers. It was for a message that has come to define what is expected to be the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in history.

“The central corrupting feature of our politics right now is the power of money to buy politicians so that government is captured by them, not for us,” El-Sayed said as he fielded questions from the stagefrom the stage, wearing his signature black T-shirt and blue jeans. “AIPAC will spend huge amounts of money if you’re uppity like me and you speak out of turn to beat you, and you’re seeing it play out on TV every day.”

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee and its affiliated groups have poured more than $30 million into the race in support of Stevens. It is the largest investment the organization has made in an electoral contest since launching its United Democracy Project super PAC in 2021.

“I have been very clear, consistent and transparent, and I have continued to be,” Stevens said during a recent televised debate when asked about AIPAC’s support for her campaign. “I want to see long-term peace. I want to see a two-state solution. I am deeply proud to represent one of the largest Jewish populations in a congressional district in the country.”

The stakes in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary extend far beyond the state. The winner will face Republican Mike Rogers in one of the country’s marquee general election contests, and Democrats need to win races like Michigan if they hope to take control of the Senate.

But first, Democratic voters are deciding a different question: whether the party’s future lies with its establishment, represented by Stevens, or with an ascendant progressive movement embodied by candidates like El-Sayed. The race has become a proxy fight over money in politics, the influence of pro-Israel groups such as AIPAC, and whether Democratic candidates can openly criticize U.S. support for Israel without sacrificing electability.

It is also unfolding in the shadow of Michigan’s 2024 Uncommitted movement, which turned the state into the epicenter of Democratic dissent over the war in Gaza and exposed fractures that continue to divide the party’s coalition, including an ongoing debate over how much the issue contributed to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ defeat.

We spoke with El-Sayed earlier this summer about AIPAC, electability and what he believes his race means for the future of Democratic politics.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Nearly two years ago, you joined members of the Uncommitted Movement at the Democratic National Convention asking them to have a Palestinian speak on stage. What was your involvement in that group?

I thought we needed to take a shot across the bow to remind the Biden administration that Arab and Muslim voters were an important part of his coalition, and that we would not stand by and watch him use our tax dollars to drop bombs on other people and their kids to do a genocide, and that he was at risk of losing a lot of important voters if they didn’t course correct. 

When Vice President Harris became the nominee, I was the first Arab or Muslim leader to endorse her openly. I took it on the chin, you can imagine. 

In both instances,  I was trying to lead with my values. Because if you saw this election from the eyes of a child in Detroit, where I was leading Wayne County’s Department of Health, Human, and Veteran Services, or you saw it from the eyes of a child in Gaza, Trump would be worse. 

But how does that contrast with the idea of where are now, where a number of progressive candidates who have campaigned around the issue of Palestine are winning Democratic primaries across the country?

That’s how democracy works. Democracy is supposed to work by giving the voters a choice about what vision they want. And I think voters are choosing their morals rather than political expediency.

When you started your campaign, it seemed like you had a Bernie-style approach centering on issues like Medicare for All. You even had a video where you interviewed a veteran who responded to the sinking of the Edmund Fitzgerald. When did your race become so foreign policy focused? 

My campaign is not really this heavy on foreign policy. It just happens to be what all y’all in the media want to talk to me about. 

Respectfully, you bring it up yourself sometimes.

When a $30 million super PAC spend is being dropped on your face by an organization whose key interest is something happening over there, then it would be ridiculous not to name it.  AIPAC is the biggest spender in this race by far, and that’s pretty insane. And they’re not spending to keep our money here, they’re spending to send our money there. So they’ve made it an issue, and it’s just another example of why we have to get money out of politics. Because so long as they can spend that kind of money buying attack ads against me, we are going to continue to watch as too many politicians bow out of having any kind of moral courage to keep our money here at home and actually do the things that we need here at home. 

But I’m running on getting money out of politics, putting money in your pocket, passing Medicare for all. 

It  just so happens that the question right now that everybody’s asking is, “How are you gonna pay for it?” Well, look at what we’re doing abroad. Look at this ridiculous war we never should have fought or have been fighting. Think about the genocide that we backstopped, the apartheid that continues to be done, the attempted annexation of Lebanon. Like, why? 

And what could we do with that money if we kept it here?

So all I’m saying is, if we wanna have nice things here, it’s better to use our money to do nice things here than to do bad things there. It’s not that hard. 

You mention AIPAC repeatedly in your campaign speeches, debate responses and on and I’m curious why you think calling them out resonates with voters?

AIPAC is the biggest spender in this race, so you can’t talk about money out of politics without talking about AIPAC. You just can’t. Like, it’d be like ignoring the elephant.

But this is nothing new, no?

But I want people to see it anew. Because you’re right, it’s nothing new. It is so common in our politics that we take it for granted, and that’s some ridiculous shit. Like, it’s ridiculous that we take it for granted that we have a bipartisan consensus on the idea that your US senators wanna send your money to some other country to buy bombs and tanks instead of keeping your money here. And it’s not just about Israel, by the way. It’s also Egypt. It’s also Pakistan. It’s also Saudi Arabia. It’s all of these places where we send foreign military aid where we should not.

What do you say to Democratic old heads who are, you know, might look at your campaign, might look at you and be like, “You’re just throwing some, some red meat to, to the lefties,” so to speak, when it comes to the issue of Palestine, that this is politically advantageous for you? 

People are asking two questions: what do you say you’re gonna fight for, and then do I believe that you’re gonna fight for it? The Democratic Party brand is in the shitter because nobody actually believes that we’re gonna show up and fight for the things that we say we wanna fight for. You know why? Because we say we’re for human rights, and then we watch them get viciously violated, and then we say nothing. So what that tells me is you’re gonna back down. So I would tell them, how about our party finds some courage, and I’m just telling you exactly what I believe, come what may. So when we beat $50 million of spending from AIPAC, I’d love to have a conversation with them. 

What do you think Palestine or Israel or the two of them together symbolize for this year’s midterms?

Moral Rorschach test.  Are you someone who is willing to be courageous and truthful, or are you someone who is willing to bend to money and power? And people are showing themselves in real time.

What do you say to people that think you are being divisive in your rhetoric, and that if you’re trying to coalition build, being this brash or loud only hurts your cause?

I’m building a coalition on the truth. And sometimes when a coalition is built on falsehood, you have to make sure that you can move it to the truth. And I’m finding that we’re building a much bigger coalition than the one that they think, you know, we’re breaking apart, because a lot of people wanna be a part of the truth. They want their kids to have good healthcare. They want to be able to travel good roads. They want good schools, and they wanna know that our tax dollars aren’t hurting other people.

What do you think the outcome of your race will say about the future of the party? 

A lot. I think everybody and their mom running for president is watching this race with a very keen eye. And if we can demonstrate that campaigning on, on truth and on courage can win in Michigan, it can win anywhere.

 If I prove that you can win statewide, taking on AIPAC and winning, that is catastrophic  because of what it says about the future of the party. It is existential to oppose it. I think this race is going to change a lot of minds, and it’s going to scramble a lot of expectations.

This interview was originally conducted as part of an upcoming episode of Reveal, slated for release later this September about the role Israel has in reshaping American politics. 

Subscribe to Reveal wherever you get your podcasts to hear the conversation and many more around this topic and other news of the day.

news.title: In Pelosi’s district, a battle over the future of San Francisco Democrats emerges
news.text:
The pair is set to debate on Oct. 1, a bit over a month out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

A changing San Francisco

The contest comes at a defining moment for San Francisco.

The city remains overwhelmingly Democratic. In 2024, Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, a local-girl-made-good of sorts after rising from San Francisco district attorney to vice president, beat President Donald Trump in the 11th Congressional District 82% to 14%. The city and district are so blue that a pair of Democrats emerged from the June 2 all-party primary, with Wiener nabbing 40.7% to Chan’s 29.7%.

But San Francisco voters recently have shown increasing frustration with some of the policies associated with its progressive wing. The 2022 recall of progressive District Attorney Chesa Boudin, amid concerns over crime, homelessness, and drug addiction, served as a major warning sign for the Left.

The city’s Democratic Mayor Daniel Lurie has embraced a more centrist approach to homelessness, addiction, downtown revitalization, and public safety, helping build a political operation that backs more moderate policies.

At the heart of the Pelosi succession fight is a deeper question: Is San Francisco changing, and if so, what does that mean for the kind of Democrat it wants representing the city in Washington?

Wiener has the opportunity to argue that he represents that evolution without abandoning San Francisco’s liberal identity. Chan can make the case that the city’s progressive values remain intact and that Pelosi’s endorsement signals continuity with the political legacy of one of the most consequential Democrats in modern American history.

The stakes are also personal and institutional. Pelosi did not initially endorse Wiener, despite his long record in San Francisco politics, and instead backed Chan just days before the June 2 primary election. Her campaign involvement has been substantial, including fundraising and appearances with Chan. Now one of Pelosi’s top aides, communications director Ian Krager, is taking a leave of absence to join Chan’s campaign, another indication of how much of Pelosi’s political operation is lining up behind her chosen successor.

Yet the race is about more than Pelosi’s blessing. It shows a wider debate that has changed San Francisco politics over the past several years, as concerns about affordability, public safety, and the city’s post-pandemic revival have competed with the progressive agenda that dominated local politics for much of the last decade.

Despite their ideological differences, political experts interviewed by the Washington Examiner largely agreed on one point: the race is not about whether San Francisco stays a liberal city. Instead, they say, it is about whether Democratic voters now place a higher premium on governing effectiveness than ideological identity.

“This race asks whether San Francisco wants a Democrat focused primarily on progressive ideology or one focused on delivering results,” political strategist James Christopher said. “It’s a debate over progressive versus pragmatic politics.”

Democratic strategist Nick Smith, who previously worked in Bay Area politics, called the contest “a race over whether San Francisco Democrats want to continue the political era Nancy Pelosi helped define or embrace a different governing approach.”

Two visions of Democratic politics 

Wiener, who grew up in New Jersey and moved to San Francisco in 1997 after graduating from Harvard Law School, cuts a familiar swath as a veteran of local and state politics, and with a 6-foot-7 frame that makes him a standout in most crowds. Wiener has sought to position himself as a congressional candidate focused on practical public policy solutions without abandoning progressive ideology. It’s an approach Wiener took during his nearly six-year tenure on the San Fransico Board of Supervisors, where he earned a reputation as a relatively business-friendly local lawmaker amid hardcore left-wingers.

Wiener was elected to the state Senate in 2016. Throughout his time in Sacramento, he has championed aggressive housing construction, arguing that the city’s housing shortage has fueled both its affordability crisis and homelessness. He has also pushed measures designed to expand public transit, address climate change, and strengthen protections for LGBT residents, while taking more centrist positions on policing and public safety.

Wiener’s campaign did not respond to a set of questions repeatedly sent by the Washington Examiner.

Analysts say Wiener is not asking voters to abandon progressive politics, but to judge government by its performance.

“Wiener isn’t trying to turn San Francisco into Orange County,” California Republican strategist Matt Klink said. “His message is that voters can remain progressive without accepting dysfunctional government.”

Chan has countered that San Francisco’s affordability problems cannot be solved through market-rate housing alone. She has built her political brand around tenant protections, labor issues, neighborhood preservation, and the expansion of affordable housing. Her campaign has emphasized protecting working-class residents from displacement while resisting what progressives describe as an increasingly corporate approach to city government.

Chan’s biography may also resonate with voters in San Francisco, where the Chinese-American community accounts for 21% of the city’s population.

Chan was born Chan Sze-man in British Hong Kong, and her family moved to Taiwan when she was five years old. Her family emigrated to the United States when Chan was 13, settling in San Francisco’s Chinatown. She graduated from the University of California, Davis, and was an aide to several local politicians in San Francisco before winning a seat on the Board of Supervisors in 2020. Known as a progressive voice on that often-fractious body, Chan is now looking to take her approach national in the rare opening for the congressional seat.

“Connie Chan has spent her career fighting for working families and taking on a rigged system that puts the interests of billionaires and big corporations ahead of the people,” campaign spokeswoman Julie Edwards said in a statement to the Washington Examiner.

“As an immigrant, a working mom, and a dedicated public servant, she has earned the trust of a broad coalition by showing up, listening to San Franciscans, standing up to Donald Trump’s destructive agenda, and delivering for working people,” Edwards said. “That’s the fight she’s led in San Francisco — and it’s the fight she’ll bring to Washington.”

Some political analysts have warned against overstating an ideological divide between Wiener and Chan. Their views largely align with each other and mainstream Democratic opinion.

“I reject the idea that this is fundamentally an ideological race,” said Mike Todaro, co-chairman of the California Forward Party, the state chapter of the national Forward Party, a centrist third-party movement. “Wiener and Chan agree on most major social issues.” Instead, Todaro argues, the contest is primarily about competing approaches to housing policy and how government should finance progressive priorities.

Yet, the divide mirrors a larger debate within the Democratic Party between elected officials who prioritize accelerating housing construction, versus progressives who say stronger tenant protections and affordability requirements must come first.

While both candidates occupy the left side of the national political spectrum, their records illustrate two distinct governing philosophies that have frequently clashed in San Francisco Democratic politics.

Pelosi’s endorsement has merely heightened those contrasts. Her decision to campaign publicly for Chan surprised some observers, given Wiener’s years of legislative experience and prominence in California Democratic politics. The endorsement also signaled that Pelosi views Chan as the candidate best positioned to continue her political legacy in a district she represented since winning a June 1987 special election.

Christopher argued the race matters not only because of who succeeds Pelosi, but as a sign of what vision of the Democratic Party that person represents.

Whether Pelosi’s endorsement ultimately proves decisive remains an open question.

What San Francisco voters want

San Francisco elections in recent years have produced mixed signals. Voters recalled Boudin, rejected several progressive school board members, and elected Lurie on promises to improve basic city services and restore confidence in local government. At the same time, they continue overwhelmingly to elect Democrats and remain supportive of progressive priorities on issues such as abortion rights, climate policy, and LGBT protections.

Smith argued that the race is ultimately less a referendum on progressive ideology than on whether city government has produced results. He said many voters still embrace progressive values but have grown skeptical that City Hall has delivered on housing, homelessness, public safety, and other quality-of-life concerns.

For Wiener, the path to victory likely depends on persuading voters that San Francisco can remain deeply liberal while pursuing a more results-oriented style of governance. For Chan, success depends on convincing voters that the city’s challenges do not require abandoning the progressive politics that have long identified it.

Political operatives say the implications could extend well beyond San Francisco.

OPINION: THE MAMDANI LEFT ISN’T GOVERNING — IT’S CLOUT CHASING

A Wiener victory, Smith said, would suggest Democratic voters are rewarding governing effectiveness over continuity. Klink argued it would show that San Francisco liberals still embrace progressive values but increasingly expect measurable results from government.

A Chan victory, by contrast, would suggest the city’s progressive coalition remains durable despite years of debate over crime, homelessness, and affordability while strengthening Pelosi’s influence over the city’s Democratic electorate. It would also indicate that voter frustration with quality-of-life issues has not fundamentally reshaped San Francisco’s political identity.

Barnini Chakraborty (@Barnini) is a senior political reporter at the Washington Examiner.

news.title: Kamala Harris backs major changes to the Supreme Court, Electoral College ahead of possible 2028 campaign
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Friday embraced a series of progressive policy proposals she did not campaign on in 2024, including expanding the Supreme Court and abolishing the Electoral College, as she continues weighing a potential 2028 presidential bid. Speaking at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville, Tenn., Harris endorsed several proposals she did not publicly campaign on during her 2024 White House run. "We must allow for a real conversation about revisiting certain things," Harris said. "I know this is gonna be controversial coming from me, in particular. We need to revisit the Electoral College." Perfectly built?

Does that sound like an objective arbiter of news to you?

Most American Jews belong to neither the camp that supports Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unconditionally nor the one that blamed Israel immediately after the October 7 massacre, J Street chief policy officer Ilan Goldenberg told i24NEWS, arguing that his organization reflects the views of the quieter majority between those poles.

Goldenberg, a former Middle East adviser to Harris who was born in Jerusalem, described himself as a liberal Zionist with a strong personal attachment to Israel. Supporting Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, he argued, does not require agreement with the conduct of its government.

He attributed the growing divide between Israel and the Democratic Party partly to Netanyahu’s increasing identification with Republican politics, beginning with his publicized clashes with former president Barack Obama over the Iran nuclear agreement and continuing through his close relationship with President Donald Trump. 

Goldenberg rejected the claim that J Street had pulled the Democratic Party too far to the left. Instead, he said the organization now finds itself arguing both with groups that support the Israeli government without qualification and with activists calling for an end to the US-Israel relationship.

J Street continues to support Israeli missile defense and a bilateral security relationship, he said, while maintaining that US weapons transfers must comply with American law. news.title: Kamala Harris snubs Biden when asked to name ‘most effective’ US presidents at Nashville event
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris awkwardly snubbed Joe Biden when she was asked who she thought were the “most effective presidents in American history.”

The one-term veep was tasked with answering the question during her appearance at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville Friday before naming Franklin Roosevelt as her top choice — failing to mention her executive partnership.

“Oh Marc, don’t make me do that,” Harris told NUL President Marc Morial before launching into a ramble of an NPR feature on the 32nd president.

“It was, of course, his three terms in office and it was interesting to … and of course the role of his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt, and you know he did some good things. In fact, it was he who talked about the expansion of the Supreme Court and then he got ferocious blowback for that,” she said.

“He did good, Social Security it was, you know, when I think about what he did in terms of investing in the people during dire times and talking about the role and responsibility of government that it should not just be about the benevolence of community organizations or or or just interpersonal relationships that the government has a role,” Harris said.

“I think that he was a very important president. He, he appreciated that government has in my mind three essential functions, which is public health, public safety and public education,” she said matter-of-factly.

The 61-year-old then named John F. Kennedy and his vice president and eventual successor, Lyndon B. Johnson, to her list of three

“Given more time to think about it, I credit Kennedy, of course, in terms of what he laid the groundwork for and then Johnson followed up on around having the ability,” she said.

After naming her three, Harris name-dropped Barack Obama, which prompted a loud ovation from the audience for the 44th president.

“And of course Barack Obama and what he did with the Affordable Care Act, among many things, but in particular the. If we had one issue that has been ailing America for generations, which is a health care system that has failed anyone other than the rich and addressing that in the way that he did and took a lot of heat for it,” she said.

Harris did not mention Biden in her response, a glaring omission after the two had a not-so-private falling out since her failed presidential campaign in 2024.

The former president, who had dropped out of his own reelection campaign 107 days before Election Day, quickly endorsed Harris as the Democratic Party nominee.

After Harris lost both the Electoral College Vote and the Popular Vote to President Trump, she cast blame against the octogenarian for a multitude of issues she claimed sunk her attempt at the White House.

“When Republicans mischaracterized my role as ‘border czar,’ no one in the White House comms team helped me to effectively push back and explain what I had really been tasked to do, nor to highlight any of the progress I had achieved,” she wrote in her book “107 Days.”

“Instead, I shouldered the blame for the porous border, an issue that had proved intractable for Democratic and Republican administrations alike,” she added.

During her appearance in Music City Friday, Harris teased what her potential 2028 presidential campaign would look like – signaling she’d support abolishing the Electoral College and packing the Supreme Court – an indication she has moved further to the left since her time on the ballot.

“I know this is going to be controversial coming from me, in particular,” she said. “We need to revisit the Electoral College. We need to revisit the point of expanding the court, to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts. We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and DC.”

Iranian cyber operations have previously targeted US infrastructure. It was inevitable that, at some stage, America’s populist Left would try to do to the Democratic Party what the populist Right has already done to the Republican Party: take it over.

Maybe now is the time their dreams will come true. Their chosen vehicle for the takeover bid is an organisation called Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

The DSA may have been around for almost 50 years, but throughout its existence it has been a political irrelevance. ‘Socialism’ has always been something of a dirty word in US politics, too akin to communism, too redolent of the old world (Europe).

Mainstream Democrats have always shunned it. Yet, remarkably, it is now part of the US political lexicon as never before.

The DSA has burgeoned since Donald Trump was re-elected in 2024. With more than 120,000 members – a majority of them new recruits – plus many tens of thousands more who regard themselves as ‘DSA adjacent’, it is now the largest explicitly socialist movement in American history. It’s not a third party. It contests Democratic primaries, which choose the party’s candidates, backing upstart radicals against old, complacent incumbents.

Its $9million annual budget is peanuts by US political standards but it can count on an army of activists and it has already scored some remarkable successes. The DSA concentrates its efforts on heavily Democratic areas where, if you win the party’s primary nomination, you’re a shoo-in come the real election.

Its poster boy, of course, is Zohran Mamdani, the young, charismatic, self-styled socialist who won last year’s Democratic primary for mayor of New York, which he duly became in January.

Mamdani is to DSA what Trump is to MAGA: its most famous face and champion. Three Mamdani-backed radicals have recently ousted incumbent Democrats in New York congressional primaries for safe seats. This means, inevitably, they’ll be in the next House of Representatives.

Mainstream Democrats have been quick to claim the DSA’s appeal is limited to the liberal elites of America’s coastal cities. But its candidates have also won primaries in places far away from the coast, including Arizona, Colorado, Georgia, North Carolina, Vermont and Utah. It claims almost 40 wins, so far, in various primaries for both state and federal elections.

Its biggest test comes on Tuesday in, of all places, Michigan, a no-nonsense, mid-western, blue-collar state which voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024 (but only just, both times).

The incumbent Democratic senator has decided not to run again. So the primary is a straight fight between a rather run-of-the-mill mainstream Democratic congresswoman, Haley Stevens, and Abdul El-Sayed, rising star of the DSA-aligned Democrats.

El-Sayed is a classic case of America’s new breed of socialist. The son of an Egyptian immigrant engineer, he’s a Muslim who was brought up in an affluent Detroit suburb.

After winning a full scholarship to study medicine at the University of Michigan, he received a prestigious Rhodes Scholarship to attend Oriel College, Oxford, where he captained the lacrosse team. He then completed his medical studies at Columbia, one of the select group of Ivy League universities.

So we’re not talking about some horny-handed son of toil here. But then it has been a long time since the Democrats were the party of America’s working class. Today’s Democratic Party base is white-collar, educated, middle-class, metropolitan – and generally unhappy with life.

Education levels are now the best predictor of how Americans will vote. In 2024, Trump won 29 of the 30 states with the lowest share of university graduates. His Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris (remember her?), won 14 of the 15 states with the highest share of university graduates.

There’s an added twist to explain the DSA’s growing popularity. Rather than dwelling on the perceived exploitation of the workers – the traditional Marxist pitch – today’s US socialists appeal to the grievances of the young, educated metropolitan classes whose liberal arts degrees have not equipped them for careers at a time when artificial intelligence is gobbling up so many entry-level jobs.

Though from affluent backgrounds, they do not feel well off themselves. Poor salaries, high housing costs and sticky inflation have seen to that.

A downwardly mobile life beckons, and that scares them. It is on such sentiments that modern US socialism preys. Solutions are another matter. The DSA can make our own loony Left sound quite sensible.

Its online manifesto calls for the destruction of the ‘capitalist oligarchy’ and a ‘socialist future’, the abolition of prisons and police, the defunding of the US military and closure of all overseas bases, a 32-hour working week (with no pay cuts, of course), universal free housing, rent controls (why would they be needed if housing was free?), public ownership of ‘essential industries’ and the ‘largest corporations’, and an end to border controls.

Plus the ripping apart of the US constitution. The Senate would be abolished, as would the Presidency and the Supreme Court, to be replaced by an executive and judiciary under the control of the House of Representatives – a sort of new ‘people’s parliament’.

Michigan’s El-Sayed is trying not to run on any of this. After all, he wants to beat not just the Democratic opponents in the primary but his Republican candidate come November.

He still has a lot of explaining to do. When riots raged in US cities after the death of George Floyd in 2020 he said the police should be defunded (he now says he was just using the language that was ‘in vogue’ at the time).

He also once described a moderate Democratic senator as ‘an ogre’ whose head he’d like to put ‘on a pike’ to intimidate other moderates.

He’s also cosied up to Hasan Piker, a notorious hard-Leftist who has opined that ‘America deserved 9/11’ and described Chairman Mao, the Chinese despot whose policies killed more than 40million, as ‘one of the great leaders of this world’.

Piker is also pro-Hamas. El-Sayed may not be that. But he calls Israel a ‘rogue state’, accuses it of ‘genocide’ and wants the US to ban further arms sales to it. This is significant. Deep hostility to Israel, often spilling into outright anti-Semitism, is in the DNA of DSA activists. Whatever policy disagreements they may have, a loathing of Israel unites them.

Just as a previous generation of young people was radicalised by the Vietnam War, so the DSA has been radicalised by Israel’s response in Gaza to the Hamas atrocities of October 7. It is what really fires them up, far more than any domestic agenda.

Republicans see a ‘Get out of jail free’ card here. If the shrill, extreme voice of the DSA is increasingly the voice of the Democrats, then perhaps November’s midterms won’t be quite the bloodbath for Trump and his party they fear. Well, maybe. But three polls this week all put Trump’s approval below 35 per cent, an all-time low.

More than 70 per cent think he’s handling the economy (the number one issue) badly and almost 75 per cent disapprove of his flailing war on Iran. Republican voter morale has slumped. Many have indicated they just won’t bother to vote come November.

The Democrats, of course, are not in much better shape. Their approval rating is as low as Trump’s. The party is still run by a gerontocracy that hasn’t had an original idea or candidate with widespread appeal for years. At least the DSA is clearing out the dead wood, at last. Even moderate Democrats acknowledge that.

US socialism still has some way to go before it becomes mainstream, if it ever does. But voters increasingly disillusioned with Trump and mainstream Democrats could easily look past their daft ideas and give them their votes – just for the hell of it.

In a sense, it’s hard to blame them. Traditional Democrats have run out of steam and purpose. Trump has started another forever war of the sort he was elected to avoid. People see him, rightly, as indifferent to the crippling cost-of-living crisis ordinary families are enduring.

Meanwhile, the kleptocracy that is the First Family and their hangers on stuff their own pockets with a level of greed that would shame a medieval monarch. If you wonder why socialism, of all things, is suddenly on the march in America – that’s the answer.
